Goal: Factorize a matrix into a product of three matrices
which share a common small dimension r.

Although there are two dimensions to the data, there is
really one effective dimension! How do we uncover
this dimension?

Find the direction
that captures the
most variance

Find the direction
that minimizes
projection error

We want to reduce the dimensions so that:
• The first dimension is the direction of greatest variance.
• Second dimension is orthogonal to the first and has the
second greatest variance.
• And so on…

Rank(A) = number of linearly independent columns/rows
of A.

• Rank(A)=2
• Row 1 = Row 2 + Row 3
• Basis: { −𝟐𝟐, −𝟑𝟑, 𝟏𝟏, 𝟑𝟑, 𝟓𝟓, 𝟎𝟎}
• New coordinates of A: [1 1], [1 0], [0 1].
Each entry is the number of items sold each day

• SVD gives a way to factorize a matrix into a product of
three smaller matrices.

• Constraints on the form of each matrix factor results in a
unique factorization (upto sign)
• We choose the latent dimension r to minimize
reconstruction error (equivalent to maximizing variance).

How to Sample the Rows and
Columns?

• With CUR decomposition, we still hope to have a small
difference in Frobenius norm 𝐴𝐴−𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶
𝐹𝐹.

• Idea:
• Define the importance of a row or column of 𝐴𝐴to be
the square of its Frobenius norm.
• When constructing 𝑅𝑅and 𝐶𝐶, sample rows and
columns of 𝐴𝐴with probability proportional to their
importances.

• Example: [3,4,5] has importance 50, [1,0,3] has importance
10.  Sample [3,4,5] with 5 times the probability of [1,0,3]

Note this is a randomized algorithm, same
column can be sampled more than once

CUR is more likely to pick points far away from the origin.
• Assuming no outliers and some smoothness, these are the
directions of maximal variation.

Example: 2 data clouds at an angle
• SVD will choose 2 orthogonal axes, thus the principal axis
will be between the 2 clouds.
• CUR will find the 2 clouds.

CUR: Provably good approx.
to SVD
